description: The "Waze for Deforestation": Currently, those who destroy the forest use cloud cover and smoke to hide their crimes from standard satellites for months, while the slow process of gathering evidence prevents swift intervention. the idea leverages NASA radarm which monitors everything 24/7, regardless of weather conditions,to generate comprehensive dossiers with a single click. This allows citizens to turn weeks of waiting into mere seconds, demanding action before the damage becomes irreversible
summary:
Every year, land degradation threatens vital biodiversity, soil fertility, and carbon sinks, largely because spatial warnings remain isolated from the institutions capable of reversing the damage.

Climate Sentinel is an open-source platform that leverages NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data to detect desertification across different stages of severity—from early signals to advanced degradation—and turn satellite intelligence into on-the-ground action. We connect these critical areas directly to restoration companies and NGOs for physical soil and vegetation recovery, link projects to carbon credit managers and buyers to fund verified climate impact, and provide public agencies with actionable frameworks to enable and scale cross-sector partnerships. 

By combining 2026 NISAR L2 GCOV radar data (HV backscatter in dB, standardized per municipality using a single orbit and frame) with MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI time series (2001–2024), CHIRPS rainfall, ERA5-Land temperature, and MapBiomas Collection 10 land-use maps, we identify critical degradation hotspots. In our comparative and explanatory module, we apply RESTREND (rainfall-adjusted NDVI trends) with Mann-Kendall testing to isolate true degradation drivers. Aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goal 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), Climate Sentinel acts as a multi-sector hub.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Climate Sentinel detects desertification hotspots then translates complex science into ready-to-fund action plans and direct partnerships for ecological restoration.

This program is an open-source web platform that alerts potential desertification regions across different severity levels (from early signs of degradation to advanced critical hotspots) and connects these regions to partners capable of reversing the situation. The platform is structured around interactive spatial exploration, scientific transparency, and an operational connection workflow:

Interactive Territorial Exploration: Where users apply analytical filters (risk category, impact type, territory size, and chart classification) to inspect historical vegetation trajectories and current structural surface conditions.

Spotlight Panel: For each selected territory, Climate Sentinel displays a Transition Risk score (It is a 0–100 score that measures how close a territory is to crossing an irreversible tipping point into severe desertification, translating complex radar and satellite data into a simple urgency index for immediate action.), along with estimated carbon credits (tCO2e), the cost of inaction (expected loss), and the cost of prevention, helping public managers justify municipal plans, budgets, and parliamentary amendments.

Ask Sentinel: An AI agent designed to explain to any user what this data means and answer questions about it. She can also be used to discuss the action plan: if an user feels the proposed action plan might not be efficient, they can talk to Sentinel to adjust the plan according to local challenges.

Explainable AI & Scientific Validation: To ensure transparency, we apply SHAP (Explainable AI) to reveal exact model drivers and RESTREND (rainfall-adjusted NDVI trends) with Mann-Kendall testing to isolate human-induced degradation from natural climate variability.

Incentivized Restoration: Priority areas display the estimated carbon credit potential (tCO2e and expected value in US dollars) through ecological restoration. Through the dedicated partner onboarding workflow (Become a Partner), restoration companies and NGOs (such as InPlanet or Unilever) connect directly to priority areas with proven impact and a clear pathway to generating carbon credits.

Newsletter: Institutions can configure custom monitoring criteria to receive automatic email alerts only when the trend, risk, or impact actually changes in the chosen territory.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact of the project?

Sentinel turns raw radar signals into measurable real-world recovery. Directly addressing the challenge's goal of translating complex radar observations into accessible, open-source insights for diverse audiences — and anchored in UN Sustainable Development Goal 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), alongside SDG 15 (Life on Land) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) — Climate Sentinel turns surface change detection into measurable real-world impact.

Raw SAR backscatter is difficult for non-specialists to interpret. Climate Sentinel translates physical radar signals (such as HV cross-polarization and the HV/HH ratio, which track woody biomass loss) into: -intuitive multi-scale dashboards (Explore) - transparent AI explanations (SHAP), and - natural-language guidance (Ask Sentinel)

This translation is tailored to four key groups:

  1. Resource Managers & Public Sector: Provides mayors, governors, and advisors with defensible risk scores, cost comparisons between inaction and prevention, and ready-to-use action plans to justify municipal budgets and policies.
  2. Partner Companies & NGOs: Closes the execution gap by connecting degraded territories to physical restoration operators and carbon credit buyers, making ecological regeneration financially viable without relying solely on public funding.
  3. Educators, Press & Civil Society: Offers researchers, journalists, and NGOs an open methodology, explicit scientific limitations, and permanent URLs to accurately communicate environmental changes.
  4. Remote Monitors & Local Communities: Protects water resources, soil fertility, agricultural resilience, and biodiversity by replacing alert fatigue with event-driven notifications (Newsletter) triggered only when real surface degradation occurs.

Climate Sentinel demonstrates how continuous NISAR time series can serve as an open Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) infrastructure, enabling governments and carbon markets to audit on-the-ground restoration progress over time and intervene before ecosystems cross critical tipping points.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Data, Tools & Tech Stack To guarantee scientific rigor, reproducibility, and modern web accessibility, our platform integrates multi-sensor Earth observation datasets with a full-stack geospatial architecture:

  • Radar & Optical Earth Observation: NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV (provisional Jun–Oct 2026 dry season; HV and HH backscatter in dB, HV/HH ratio, texture, temporal variation, and soil moisture sensitivity, standardized per municipality using a single orbit and frame) as our primary structural validation reference, alongside MODIS (MOD13Q1/MOD13A3 NDVI, 2001–2024), Landsat, and Sentinel-1/OPERA reference layers. Incorporating NISAR confirms historical MODIS degradation (0.77 AUC), boosts detector performance from 0.72 to 0.82, and provides 55% of the model's total explanatory power (mean |SHAP| importance of 2.18, compared to 0.98 for optical history and 0.81 for climate).
  • Climate, Rainfall & Territorial Baselines: CHIRPS, GPM IMERG, ERA5-Land, and NASA POWER for precipitation and climate reanalysis, combined with MapBiomas Collection 10 for land-use classification and IBGE municipal boundaries.
  • Geospatial Processing & Machine Learning (Python): Data ingestion via NASA Earthdata (earthaccess) and Google Earth Engine, processed with xarray, rioxarray, rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj, NumPy, and pandas. Predictive modeling and explainability are powered by scikit-learn, XGBoost, and SHAP (alongside RESTREND and Mann-Kendall statistical testing).
  • Frontend & Interactive Mapping: Built with Next.js, React, TypeScript/TSX, Tailwind CSS, and Leaflet (platform/), complemented by JavaScript/HTML/CSS web interfaces (web/) and Streamlit/Folium interactive comparison tools.
  • Backend, Spatial Database & Infrastructure: FastAPI and Uvicorn REST API backed by PostgreSQL with PostGIS for spatial storage and querying, containerized with Docker and Docker Compose, and deployed via Nginx and Easypanel.
  • AI & Automated Alerts: Google Gemini for generating tailored restoration and policy recommendations, Microsoft Foundry (via OpenAI-compatible API) powering the Ask Sentinel conversational assistant, and Brevo SMTP for automated, event-driven email notifications.
  • Design, Workflow & AI-Assisted Development: Figma for UX design, wireframing, and interface prototyping; Trello for agile task management and workflow tracking; Cursor as an AI-powered code editor to build and refine front-end components; and Google Gemini for research, data synthesis, copy drafting, and technical support during development.

Github Repository

Creativity & Innovation

Climate Sentinel turns NISAR radar into a self-sustaining restoration marketplace that connects at-risk municipalities directly with restoration operators and carbon buyers. Most remote sensing applications stop at passive monitoring — displaying a static map of past degradation without showing what to do next. Climate Sentinel innovates by using NISAR radar data as an operational engine for action plans and multi-stakeholder partnerships (UN SDG 17). By combining 23 years of climate-adjusted optical trends with 2026 L-band structural radar, model explainability via SHAP, inaction-vs-prevention cost modeling, and soil carbon valuation, our platform translates raw backscatter directly into ready-to-execute public policy plans and an active bridge connecting municipalities, restoration companies/NGOs, and carbon credit buyers — turning satellite observation into a collaborative, self-sustaining regeneration ecosystem.

What factors did your team consider?

When designing Climate Sentinel, our team prioritized four core factors: scientific reliability, financial feasibility, accessibility for non-specialists, and operational sustainability.

Scientifically, we accounted for seasonal climate variability and radar geometry biases by standardizing NISAR L-band observations per municipality using a single orbit and frame during the dry season, and by combining 23 years of MODIS optical data with RESTREND and Mann-Kendall tests to isolate human-induced degradation from natural droughts—while explicitly displaying scientific limitations to prevent false-positive policy decisions. Economically, recognizing that municipalities often lack budgets for large-scale restoration, we modeled the cost of inaction versus prevention alongside carbon credit potential to attract private restoration partners and NGOs. From a usability standpoint, because raw SAR backscatter is complex for decision-makers, we integrated SHAP explainability, a 0–100 Transition Risk score, and the Ask Sentinel AI agent to translate technical metrics into actionable local plans. Finally, to prevent alert fatigue among local monitors and institutions, we designed an event-driven notification system that triggers alerts only when significant surface or risk changes occur.
